note: Every external claim of the README comes from one of these pages. 'used' = something of it is in the pipeline; every glyph and frame is drawn from paths in src/, with no third-party artwork and no icon font.

sources.name: milsymbol
sources.facts: Generates military unit symbols as SVG or canvas from a SIDC code; implements MIL-STD-2525C/D/E, FM 1-02.2 and STANAG APP-6 B/D/E; options include size, fill, frame, colorMode (Light/Medium/Dark), monoColor, outlineWidth, stack; modifiers include echelon, headquarters, task force, dummy/feint.
sources.decision: Not used and NOT executed or downloaded. Evaluated from its repository files only. It needs a SIDC per symbol, so the 1863 vocabulary (horse artillery, sharpshooters, formations with no arm) would have to be mapped onto standard codes; its symbol sets were not enumerated. Its options include a stack effect, but the pages read show no count slot, arm-set row, carried-forward state or atlas output. As a BUILD-TIME source it could back a strict APP-6 language through the language registry (src/languages.mjs); whether it would look better than the hand-drawn NATO language was not tested.
blocked: npmjs.com/package/milsymbol returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool: not worked around

sources.name: NATO Joint Military Symbology (Wikipedia)
sources.licence: CC BY-SA (Wikipedia text); facts only, no text copied
sources.facts: APP-6A frame shapes: friendly blue rectangle, hostile red diamond, neutral green square, unknown yellow quatrefoil; shape and colour are redundant; infantry = saltire, cavalry/reconnaissance = single diagonal, field artillery = cannonball symbol; MIL-STD-2525A is the US equivalent.

sources.name: NATO Unit Counter Guide (Military History Visualized)
sources.facts: Echelon marks: single line company/battery, two lines battalion, three lines regiment, X brigade, XX division, XXX corps, XXXX army.

sources.name: NATO Map Symbols (army.ca wiki)
sources.facts: Describes the enemy frame as an inverted pentagon, which conflicts with the APP-6A diamond on Wikipedia; unresolved, not relied on. The README says the diamond here means 'the other army', not 'hostile'.
